intro:
By the end of this track you can write Kotlin coroutine code that you can trust when many things happen at once. A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause without holding a thread, like a dish a cook leaves to simmer while she starts the next one. You can say what `suspend` does and doesn't do, start several slow calls together so they take only as long as the slowest, and keep every coroutine inside a scope that waits for it, cancels it and hears about its failures. You can put blocking calls and CPU work on the right dispatcher, make loops and blocking calls hear a cancel, and let independent work fail alone. You can build cold flows, share hot ones with StateFlow and SharedFlow, pass work between coroutines through channels, guard shared state with a Mutex, and test all of it on a fake clock. And you can connect coroutines to `CompletableFuture`, Reactor and virtual threads, and choose between the three.

One picture runs through the whole track: a home cook making a big dinner. The cook is a thread, and each dish on the go is a coroutine. The bookmark in the recipe is what lets a dish pause, a course goes out only when all its dishes are ready, and when the guests call dinner off, the cook hears it only between steps. The cheat sheet below puts each picture next to its code.

You need everyday Kotlin; the earlier tracks help, but each lesson explains what it uses. Install JDK 25. The library is kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0 with Kotlin 2.4.21, and the lessons say which version a fact comes from, because several rules changed recently: passing a `Job` to a builder is deprecated since 1.11, and explicit backing fields became stable in Kotlin 2.4. The labs live in `labs/coroutines`, one package per lesson (`workbench.coroutines.l01` to `l11`), all in Kotlin, with one Java test in lesson 11 that calls the Kotlin code from Java. Most starting files are buggy code with a KDoc that says what is wrong; a few are `TODO()`s. From `labs/`, run `./gradlew :coroutines:test --tests 'workbench.coroutines.lNN.*'` until it passes, and `solutionTest` to check the reference answers. Nearly every test runs on virtual time with `runTest`, so a test of a 30-second wait finishes in milliseconds. The Try-it demos run with `./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=...`, and almost every Kotlin demo has a Java twin with the closest Java equivalent.
cheatsheet:
## The picture

A home cook makes a big dinner. The cook is a **thread**, the worker that runs code. Each dish on the go is a **coroutine**: it can pause, with a bookmark in the recipe (the continuation), while the kitchen timer runs (`delay`), and the cook starts something else. A course goes out only when all its dishes are ready (the job tree). When the guests call dinner off, the cook hears it only between steps (cancellation). Each row below recalls the picture from the lesson that used it.

## Suspending and builders

| You want | Use | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| A function that waits without holding its thread | `suspend fun` with `delay` or other suspend calls inside | a bookmark in the recipe while the timer runs |
| Fire and forget inside a scope | `launch { }` returns a `Job` | start the potatoes and get on |
| A result later | `async { }` returns a `Deferred`; start them all, then `await()` | text three shops at once, then read the replies |
| Several children, wait for all, fail together | `coroutineScope { }` | a course goes out when all its dishes are ready |
| Children that fail alone | `supervisorScope { }` | one burnt tray doesn't spoil the bake sale |
| Run one step on another dispatcher and come back | `withContext(dispatcher) { }` | carry the step to the bench by the door |
| Block a thread until done: `main`, tests, a blocking edge | `runBlocking { }`, never inside suspend code | the cook stands still on purpose |
| Background work owned by a class | `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler)`, cancelled when the owner closes | an oven with an off switch |
| Wrap a one-shot callback | `suspendCancellableCoroutine { }` with `invokeOnCancellation { }` | the bakery's callback turned into a bookmark |

The tree: a parent completes only after its children; cancellation flows down; a failure (anything but `CancellationException`) cancels the parent and siblings, unless the parent is a supervisor. `GlobalScope` and a `CoroutineScope(...)` created inside a function make orphans: a pan left on in the neighbour's kitchen.

## Dispatchers and context

| Dispatcher | For | Size | Picture it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Dispatchers.Default` | CPU work; the default for `launch` and `async` | one thread per core, at least 2 | the counter, one cutting board per pair of hands |
| `Dispatchers.IO` | blocking calls (database drivers, blocking libraries) | 64 at once (or cores, if more) | the bench by the front door |
| `Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n, "name")` | one blocking resource with its own budget | n, added on top of IO's 64 | a slow shop with its own bench |
| `Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(n)` | a CPU budget | at most the core count | a share of the cutting boards |
| `executor.asCoroutineDispatcher()` | an existing pool or virtual threads; close it | whatever the executor allows | with virtual threads, a cheap helper at every pot |
| `Dispatchers.Unconfined`, `Dispatchers.Main` | library code; user-interface threads | not for server code | |

Context: the note clipped to every dish. `+` merges elements, the right side wins; children inherit everything but the `Job`. Look the dispatcher up with `ContinuationInterceptor` (1.11). A `ThreadLocal` needs `asContextElement()`.

## Cancellation

| Situation | Do | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| A CPU loop | `ensureActive()`, `yield()` or `while (isActive)` every few hundred items | the helper sorting lentils must look up now and then |
| Catching around suspend calls | rethrow `CancellationException`; `runCatching` and `catch (e: Exception)` catch it | don't throw away the message that dinner is off |
| Suspending cleanup in `finally` | `withContext(NonCancellable) { release() }` | give the borrowed pan back anyway |
| A deadline that is an expected outcome | `withTimeoutOrNull(d) { } ?: fallback` | if the bakery hasn't answered, bake your own |
| A deadline that must fail the caller | `withTimeoutOrNull(d) { } ?: error("timed out")`; `withTimeout` inside `launch` fails quietly | |
| A blocking call that should stop on cancel | `runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { }`, plus the library's own timeout | hang up on the bakery's old hotline |
| `asFlow()` over a long collection | add `.cancellable()` | |

## Exceptions

| Builder | Failure goes to | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| `launch` child | its parent at once | the smell of burnt gravy reaches everyone |
| `async` child | its parent at once, whether or not anyone awaits | the lid doesn't keep the smell in |
| root `launch` (in a scope you created, or a supervisor's child) | the `CoroutineExceptionHandler` in its context, else the uncaught handler | the notebook by the oven |
| root `async` | kept in the `Deferred`; `await()` rethrows it | |

Handlers only work on roots. Put `SupervisorJob()` in a scope's constructor or use `supervisorScope`; `launch(SupervisorJob())` detaches the child from the tree. The first exception wins, the rest are suppressed.

## Flow

| Rule | Detail | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| Cold | the `flow { }` body runs once per collector, only when collected | a recipe card cooks nothing until someone cooks from it |
| Sequential | `emit` suspends until the collector is done; `take(n)` stops the producer | one step of the card at a time |
| Operators | intermediate (`map`, `filter`, `onEach`, `take`) build; terminal (`collect`, `toList`, `first`) run | adding steps to the card vs cooking from it |
| Context | `flowOn(d)` moves everything above it; `emit` inside `withContext` throws | |
| Errors | `catch` sees only upstream; the collector's exceptions pass through; never `try` around `emit` | |
| Endings | `onCompletion { cause -> }`: `null`, the error, or a `CancellationException` for an early stop | |
| Backpressure | plain waits; `buffer()` runs ahead; `conflate()` keeps the latest; `collectLatest` cancels stale work | a slow screen on the fridge and a fast oven probe |

## Hot streams and channels

| Type | Behavior | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| `StateFlow` | one current value; conflates; skips equal values; never completes | the menu board in the hall |
| `SharedFlow` | every value to every subscriber; `replay`, `extraBufferCapacity`, `onBufferOverflow`; the default has no buffer, so `tryEmit` fails while a subscriber is busy | the house bell |
| `stateIn` / `shareIn` | one shared upstream; `SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000)` starts with the first subscriber, stops 5 s after the last | many screens, one thermometer |
| Read-only state | `val s: StateFlow<T>` with `field = MutableStateFlow(x)` (Kotlin 2.4), or `asStateFlow()`; update with `update { }` or `compareAndSet` | only the kitchen moves the dish on |
| `Channel` | a queue: each element to one receiver; rendezvous by default; close it, or `for` never ends | the hatch, and the size of its shelf |
| Fan-out / fan-in | N workers on one channel cap the work at N; close the results channel after `joinAll()` | a team of helpers at one hatch |
| `select` | the first clause to complete wins (`onAwait`, `onReceive`, `onTimeout`); biased to the first | phone two bakeries, take the first answer |
| `callbackFlow` | `trySend` from the callback, end with `awaitClose { unregister() }` | the old oven probe's listener |

## Shared state and testing

| Need | Use | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| One counter or value | `AtomicLong`, `AtomicReference`, `MutableStateFlow.update` | 100 helpers counting peas into one pot |
| A compound update | `Mutex.withLock { }`: suspends, fair, not reentrant; keep suspension outside it if you can | the pen on a string by the fridge |
| `limitedParallelism(1)` | one coroutine at a time only between suspension points: not a mutex | the pen goes down at every suspension |
| State one coroutine owns | confinement: one coroutine, requests through a channel | only one helper may touch the list |
| Fast, exact timing tests | `runTest`; `currentTime`, `advanceTimeBy`, `runCurrent`, `advanceUntilIdle` | a rehearsal dinner on a fake clock |
| Delays in the code under test | inject the dispatcher; `Dispatchers.IO` and `Default` stay real time | the rehearsal skips only its own scenes |
| A child that must start at once | `UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)` | |
| Endless work in a test | `backgroundScope`; `advanceUntilIdle` ignores it | |

## Bridges and choosing

| From | To | Use | Picture it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CompletableFuture` | suspend | `future.await()` (cancels the future); `asDeferred().await()` (doesn't) | wait for the neighbour's ticket without standing at her door |
| suspend | `CompletableFuture` | `scope.future { }` with an owned scope | hand the neighbour a ticket tied to our dish |
| suspend | `Mono` / `Flux` | `mono { }` (cold), `flux { }`, `flow.asFlux()` | a recipe card for the conveyor kitchen |
| `Mono` / `Flux` | suspend / Flow | `awaitSingle()`, `awaitSingleOrNull()`, `publisher.asFlow()` | |
| blocking Java caller | suspend | `runBlocking { withTimeout(d) { } }`, fine on a virtual thread | a door for callers who wait anyway |

Virtual threads (a cheap helper at every pot) for blocking Java code at scale; coroutines for Kotlin code that needs structured fan-out, cancellation and Flow; Reactor (a line of stations) where a reactive stack already exists. One model per part of the program, converted at its edges.
recap: `suspend` lets a function pause without blocking its thread, like a bookmark in the recipe; the dispatcher, not `suspend`, decides which thread runs it. Wrap callbacks with `suspendCancellableCoroutine`.

Every coroutine lives in a tree: parents wait for children, cancellation flows down, failures flow up. Use `coroutineScope` for work the caller waits for, an owned scope for work that outlives a call, and never `GlobalScope`.
Blocking calls go on `Dispatchers.IO` (or a `limitedParallelism` view sized to the resource), CPU work on `Default`, and `withContext` switches and comes back.
Cancellation is cooperative and travels as `CancellationException`: check in CPU loops, rethrow it from every catch-all, clean up with `NonCancellable`, and use `runInterruptible` for blocking calls.
A failed `launch` or `async` cancels its parent at once. Supervisors (`supervisorScope`, `SupervisorJob()` in a scope's constructor) let children fail alone; handlers only work on roots.
Flows are cold and sequential: `flowOn` moves the upstream, `catch` handles only upstream errors, `onCompletion` sees every ending.
StateFlow is state (conflated, no repeats); SharedFlow is events (configure its buffer); `stateIn` with `WhileSubscribed` shares one upstream.
Channels hand each element to one receiver: teams of workers, pipelines and `callbackFlow` bridges, with `select` for whichever comes first.
Guard compound updates with a `Mutex`, not a one-thread view, and test timing logic on virtual time with `runTest` and injected dispatchers.
Bridge to Java with `future { }`, `await()`, `mono { }` and `awaitSingle()`, and choose virtual threads, coroutines or Reactor per part of the program.

quiz.q: Five coroutines in one `runBlocking` each call `Thread.sleep(100)` and print a line. About how long does the program take?
options: About 100 ms, because coroutines run concurrently
About 500 ms, because `Thread.sleep` blocks the one thread they share
About 100 ms on a 4-core machine, 125 ms on 2 cores
It doesn't compile: `Thread.sleep` is not allowed in a coroutine
quiz.why: `runBlocking` runs its coroutines on the calling thread, and `Thread.sleep` blocks that thread, so the five sleeps happen one after another: the cook standing at each pot in turn. `delay(100)` would suspend instead, and the whole thing would take about 100 ms.

options: `salad done` prints at 1 s, then the scope throws
The exception is logged, and the scope returns normally at 1 s
At about 100 ms the second child is cancelled, `salad done` never prints, and the scope throws `IOException`
Nothing is thrown, because `launch` swallows exceptions
quiz.why: A failed child cancels its parent scope, which cancels the sibling and then rethrows the original exception once every child has stopped. Nothing waits for the full second.

quiz.q: A Kotlin program calls a blocking database driver from coroutines, and the database allows 20 connections. Where should the calls run?
options: `withContext(Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "db"))` inside the code that calls the driver
On `Dispatchers.Default`, because it is the default
`withContext(Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(20))`
`Dispatchers.Unconfined`, so they start immediately
quiz.why: Blocking calls belong on IO, and a view of 20 matches the connections and adds to IO's 64 instead of competing with other blocking work. Default has one thread per core and must never block; a view over Default can't exceed the core count anyway.

quiz.q: A poller runs `while (true) { runCatching { checkOven(); delay(5_000) } }`. When dinner ends, its scope is cancelled. What happens?
options: The loop ends at the next `delay`
The JVM interrupts the thread and the loop ends
The loop ends after the current check
The loop spins at full speed: every `delay` throws at once and `runCatching` swallows it
quiz.why: `runCatching` catches `CancellationException` like any other `Throwable`. The coroutine stays cancelled, so each `delay` throws immediately, gets swallowed, and the loop goes round again. Rethrow `CancellationException`, or keep the `delay` outside the catch.

quiz.q: To stop a failed thank-you text from cancelling the rest of a dinner, someone writes `launch(SupervisorJob()) { texts.send(guest) }` inside `coroutineScope`. What did they get?
options: A supervised child that the scope still waits for
A child cut loose from the tree: the scope doesn't wait for it or cancel it, and its failure goes to a handler
A compile error
The same as `supervisorScope`
quiz.why: A `Job` in a builder's context replaces the parent, so the coroutine becomes a child of a fresh SupervisorJob outside the dinner's tree. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 deprecates the pattern. Use `supervisorScope { }`, or a supervisor scope owned by a long-lived class.

quiz.q: `orders.map { parse(it) }.catch { emit(FALLBACK) }.collect { pantry.save(it) }`. `pantry.save` throws `IOException`. What does the caller of `collect` see?
options: The `IOException`
Nothing: `catch` emits `FALLBACK` and the flow continues
An `IllegalStateException` about exception transparency
`FALLBACK` saved in place of the failed order
quiz.why: `catch` only handles exceptions from above it. The save runs in the collector, below `catch`, so its exception passes straight through. Move the save into `onEach` above `catch` if the fallback should cover it.

quiz.q: Every change of a dish's status must reach both the kitchen log and the screen in the hall, and none may be lost when a callback that can't suspend publishes a burst of them. Which holder fits?
options: `MutableStateFlow<Transition?>(null)`
A cold `flow { }` that each consumer collects
`MutableSharedFlow<Transition>(extraBufferCapacity = 64)`, publishing with a checked `tryEmit`
`MutableSharedFlow<Transition>()` with default parameters and `tryEmit`
quiz.why: Events for several subscribers call for a SharedFlow, the bell, and a publisher that can't suspend needs a buffer so `tryEmit` can hand values to busy subscribers. A StateFlow, the board, conflates events away, and a default SharedFlow has no buffer, so `tryEmit` fails whenever a subscriber is busy.

quiz.q: A screen recomputes the roast's remaining time each time the oven probe sends a reading. A recompute takes 300 ms, readings arrive every 100 ms, and only the latest matters. Which operator fits?
options: `buffer()`
`conflate()`
`flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)`
`collectLatest { }`
quiz.why: `collectLatest` cancels the computation in progress when a new reading arrives, so stale work stops at once and only the latest is finished. `conflate` skips values but still finishes every computation it starts; `buffer` computes them all.

quiz.q: Helpers on `Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)` each run `val b = list["flour"]; val g = units.toGrams(1, "scoop"); list["flour"] = b + g`, where `toGrams` suspends. Which change makes it correct?
options: Mark the list as `@Volatile`
Convert first, then do the read and the write together with no suspension between them (or hold a `Mutex` across all of it)
Use `Dispatchers.Default` without the view
Add `yield()` before the write
quiz.why: A one-thread view keeps other coroutines out only between suspension points, so helpers interleave at `toGrams` and overwrite each other: the pen goes down mid-sentence. Removing the suspension from the critical part, or holding a Mutex across it, closes the gap. `@Volatile` and `yield()` don't.

quiz.q: A Java caller holds `f = door.cookAsync(order)`, built with `scope.future { cook(order) }`, and its `orTimeout(800, MILLISECONDS)` fires. What happens to the Kotlin coroutine?
options: It is cancelled, because its future completed
It keeps running, and the result is thrown away
Its thread is interrupted
The whole scope behind the door is cancelled
quiz.why: The coroutine started by `future { }` is cancelled when its future is cancelled or otherwise completed, and `orTimeout` completes that same future exceptionally. Only that coroutine stops; the scope and its other children carry on.
